lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on excellence and exposure
lead.head: Give luck a bigger target

pic.caption: Ajay Shah (left) and Amit Varma early in Episode 39

body: Remembering a night in 1988, when Tracy Chapman filled in for Stevie Wonder with an acous­tic gui­tar, brought a phrase to Amit Varma’s mind: the sur­face area of serendip­ity[[x1]].
Luck, the hosts ar­gued, is not[[x2]] pure chance. You can widen the area it can hit.

Varma cred­ited the idea to Jason Roberts and gave it a for­mula: luck equals pas­sion­ate doing mul­ti­plied by ef­fec­tive telling. In his own al­lit­er­a­tion, ex­cel­lence and ex­po­sure. {039-C01}
Chapman had both, he said: thou­sands of hours of craft be­hind songs like *Fast Car*, and the luck of being there. One with­out the other would have come to noth­ing.

Ajay Shah, as an econ­o­mist, saw a trade-off. A Jimi Hendrix who prac­tises only in the bath­room has a prob­lem. So does the mod­ern schmoozer, one of the “con­tent-free hus­tlers” who “ac­tu­ally know noth­ing”.
## Craft be­fore con­tracts
In India, Shah ar­gued, the first-order prob­lem is the craft. Many young peo­ple he meets want the re­ward set­tled be­fore the work be­gins.
“People want a locked in, vis­i­ble, clear rec­i­proc­ity that give me this big lol­lipop, and then I will put my 50,000 hours,” he said. “And that’s not how life works.” {039-C04}
He pointed to Linus Torvalds, who wrote the Linux ker­nel with no salary, prize or fame on offer. Greatness, Shah said, takes way more than the pop­u­lar 10,000 hours.
Varma was care­ful to add that in­di­vid­u­als are not to blame. Generations of scarcity, he said, built a goal-directed cul­ture with lit­tle room for any­thing higher.

There is a bet­ter loop, he said, bor­row­ing a line from the show’s crew mem­ber Nomsita: she is happy when she does things well, and does things well when she is happy. Its mir­ror is the vi­cious cycle of the en­ti­tled, in whom medi­ocrity and en­ti­tle­ment feed each other. {039-C06}
## Out of the house

Exposure comes harder to both men. Varma, a self-described clas­sic in­tro­vert, has never mar­keted the show. Yet the show found its crew the day he hap­pened to go to a Starbucks in Versova and a man he knew only on­line said hello.

Shah, also a nat­u­ral in­tro­vert, ad­mits that meet­ing new peo­ple is hard. He has learned to do it any­way, and to con­nect oth­ers across dis­ci­plines, judg­ing them by their ideas rather than their de­grees.
Varma widened the idea. Reading, watch­ing films and mak­ing things also en­large the sur­face, he said: ex­po­sure runs from the world to you as well. {039-C02}
## Less envy, more sig­nal

Shah closed with net­works. If ideas passed be­tween peo­ple with­out loss, six de­grees of sep­a­ra­tion would let a mu­si­cian play for one per­son and go back to the bath­room, “be­cause then you’re done, then Putin knows”.
“There is trans­mis­sion loss, and every pipe has lim­ited band­width,” he said. Only long-built trust lets a few sen­tences land with full force. {039-C11}
The fix, Shah said, is cul­tural. With less envy, re­sent­ment and com­pet­i­tive­ness, ideas would travel through elite net­works with less loss, and ev­ery­one would need fewer con­fer­ences.
Modern India’s elite cul­ture is still being forged, Shah said, and “the cul­ture is made up out of a mil­lion be­hav­iors”. So each of us can help to make it.

second.label: Work and reward
second.head: Lollipop first? No deal
second.deck: Ajay Shah says young Indians want the reward before they put in the years
body: Ajay Shah meets lots of young peo­ple, and he sees a pat­tern. They want a con­tract, pay and prom­ises be­fore they com­mit years of ef­fort to any­thing. {039-C04}

Linus Torvalds, he said, de­cided[[x3]] as a teenager to write a Linux ker­nel. Nobody of­fered him a salary, a job, a prize, fame or glory. Shah, who told that larger story in the show’s Unix episode, is “de­pressed and dis­ap­pointed” at how lit­tle of such work hap­pens in India. {039-R05}
Demanding a di­rect link be­tween ef­fort and out­come, he ar­gued, is the path to weak­ness and medi­ocrity. His ad­vice was sim­pler: “Do try. Because what’s the point of liv­ing if you don’t?”

quote.text: There is a lack of the inner fire and the de­vo­tion and the abil­ity to stay hun­gry

third.head: No lectures, see the blog

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on rationing his own exposure

body: Early in his ca­reer, Ajay Shah was drawn into a good cir­cuit of Indian eco­nom­ics con­fer­ences, and he is grate­ful to those who in­vited him. As the eco­nom­ics com­mu­nity de­clined, he said, many of those con­fer­ences stopped work­ing, so he grew choosier.

For years he also ac­cepted guest lec­tures, be­cause teach­ing works so badly in India. Then he built out­lets that run with­out him: the Leap Blog, which he co-edits, this show, an XKDR YouTube chan­nel, a flow of work­ing pa­pers and a fort­nightly col­umn. {039-R18}
Now he de­clines most speak­ing and teach­ing in­vi­ta­tions. “I’ve done my re­spon­si­bil­ity to the uni­verse,” he said. “I’ve built all these things, I point peo­ple to them.” {039-S06}
Anything more, he said, “would be a high op­por­tu­nity cost”.

sections.label: The opening
sections.head: The perils of the quick study
sections.caption: his biggest mistake
body: The hosts opened by ask­ing each other an un­ex­pected ques­tion. Ajay Shah’s, to Amit Varma, was: what is the big­gest mis­take of your life?[[x8]]
Varma chose a broad one: he did not work hard enough. He was lost in grand plans, he said, and built none of the pro­cesses and habits he now teaches his writ­ing stu­dents. {039-S02}

Behind it lay what he called a meta mis­take. He came to self-reflection too late. “I think most of us don’t do any self re­flec­tion and it’s tragic,” he said. Take five min­utes every day to think hon­estly about your­self, he ar­gued, and you would be amazed at what you see. {#fiveminutes}
## Verbs, not ad­jec­tives
Varma does not like the per­son he was twenty years ago. He was ar­ro­gant, he said, be­cause he could study in one hour what took oth­ers ten.
He tied it to a study dis­cussed in an ear­lier episode[[x7]]. Children praised for being smart grew en­ti­tled and stopped work­ing hard; those praised for ef­fort kept try­ing.
“In writ­ing I often say that focus on verbs, don’t focus on ad­jec­tives,” he said. “So in a very dif­fer­ent con­text, focus on verbs, focus on doing, focus on work­ing.” {039-C03}
Could he have avoided the mis­take? No, he said: he had to live and change be­fore he could even see the op­tion.
~ Shah replied with a say­ing: “Youth is wasted on the young.” Varma fin­ished it: “and wis­dom is wasted on the old.” {039-J12}

quote.text: I just didn’t work hard. I was al­ways float­ing in my head, lost in day­dreams, think­ing of grand plans

art.caption: Amit Varma on his biggest mistake

sections.label: Chapter one
sections.head: Out of the bathroom, Jimi
sections.caption: excellence times exposure
body: Amit Varma calls the two halves of luck ex­cel­lence and ex­po­sure, and be­lieves both need to be got right. Tracy Chapman, he said, spent thou­sands and thou­sands of hours be­com­ing good, but she also needed the ex­po­sure. {039-C01}

Ajay Shah, as an econ­o­mist, im­me­di­ately saw a trade-off. Being “just Jimi Hendrix prac­tic­ing gui­tar only in the bath­room”, he said, is a prob­lem. So are the “con­tent-free hus­tlers who are just try­ing to go out and schmooze”. {039-J04}
Everyone, he said, should ask where they stand, and whether to push one side up or down a lit­tle.
## Beyond 10,000 hours
In India, Shah ar­gued, the pri­mal prob­lem is the first half: peo­ple are not com­mit­ting enough to the craft, the knowl­edge, the doing.

Nor is the fa­mous 10,000 hours[[x9]] enough. That much prac­tice might get you to play *Für Elise* rea­son­ably well, he said, but cre­at­ing some­thing new is an­other level of in­ten­sity. Linus Torvalds, Ken Thompson, Chapman, Hendrix and Jimmy Page gave en­tire lives to their work. {039-C05}
Luck still plays its part. Shah quoted a song: “I don’t know why for­tune smiles on some and lets the rest go free.” You don’t con­trol it, he said: “You’ve just got to be zen about it.” {039-J16}
~ The other half of the for­mula, Shah re­called, was his father’s daily prac­tice at CMIE. That story is on page 3.

quote.text: Actually, glory and great­ness is not 10,000 hours, it is way more than that.

sections.label: Chapter two
sections.head: Round and round, up or down
sections.caption: virtuous and vicious cycles
body: Amit Varma wanted one thing clear: the hosts are not blam­ing in­di­vid­u­als. After long years of scarcity, he said, it is nat­u­ral for a cul­ture to be­come goal-directed: get into IIT, do an IIM, be­come a vice-president at Citibank.
A news­let­ter he wrote on the day of record­ing was sparked by a line from Nomsita, of the show’s crew: “I am happy when I am doing things well, and I do things well when I’m happy.”

Work done for its own sake[[x10]], he said, gives joy, and joy drives you deeper. The vi­cious cycle be­longs to the en­ti­tled: de­nied val­i­da­tion, they turn bit­ter; given it, they de­cide they never needed to work. {039-C06}
## “I have ar­rived”
Ajay Shah agreed. The most dan­ger­ous thing about being an IITian, he said, is “the sense that I have ar­rived”, which lets peo­ple stop try­ing for years.
His way out came from Richard Stallman: “a good pro­gram­mer will never starve.” A day job, Shah said, need not be your whole life. {039-J15}

Nothing gets done quickly, Shah stressed. Of young­sters who want three months on an open-source project to show GitHub on a résumé, he said: “I just want to kick them out of the of­fice that noth­ing works like that.” {039-J03}
~ The econ­omy of a mod­ern India al­lows such lives, Shah said. It is the cul­ture that has not caught up.

quote.text: It’s a vi­cious cycle where the medi­ocrity and the en­ti­tle­ment per­pet­u­ate each other.

sections.label: Chapter three
sections.head: Mavens, meet the connectors
sections.caption: mavens and connectors
body: Amit Varma calls him­self a clas­sic in­tro­vert. He has never mar­keted this show or *The Seen and the Unseen*, be­liev­ing a good prod­uct is the best mar­ket­ing[[x11]]. “Like Sartre says, hell is other peo­ple,” he said. {039-J17}

In Malcolm Gladwell’s *The Tipping Point*, mavens go deep into some­thing, while con­nec­tors go out and link peo­ple. Varma counts him­self a maven, and won­dered whether, through an act of in­ten­tion­al­ity, he should try to be more of a con­nec­tor. {039-C08}
Ajay Shah ad­mit­ted that he too strug­gles to get to know new peo­ple. All of us look brusque and prickly from a dis­tance, he said; once you get going, there are no strangers.
## Ideas, not de­grees
Mentors such as Rakesh Mohan, Suman Bery, Vijay Kelkar and Montek brought Shah into India’s eco­nom­ics com­mu­nity when he was new. He tries to do the same, in two ways of his own.
First, he ig­nores cre­den­tials. “I don’t care about Harvard, MIT, IIT, what­ever,” he said. What mat­ters is whether a per­son is ask­ing in­ter­est­ing ques­tions. {039-C09}
Second, he con­nects peo­ple across eco­nom­ics, fi­nance, pub­lic pol­icy, soft­ware and sta­tis­tics, peo­ple who would never bump into each other at a con­fer­ence by chance.
~ Earlier that day Shah had taught Varma a word for this: su­per­con­nec­tor. Varma said Shah was one.

quote.text: I don’t have the per­son­al­ity to be a con­nec­tor, to just turn to a stranger at a con­fer­ence

sections.label: The reccos
sections.head: One film every three years
sections.caption: the golden age of cinema
body: Asked for a rec­om­men­da­tion, Amit Varma said he felt in­spired, and chose a film that in­spired him at sev­en­teen or eigh­teen: Peter Weir’s *Dead Poets Society*. Just think­ing of it, es­pe­cially its last scene, made him well up. Its mes­sage, in his words: seize the day, *carpe diem*.
Ajay Shah drew a blank. “You cover up for me and pro­duce a sec­ond rec­om­men­da­tion,” he said.
## A golden age

Varma chose Justine Triet’s *Anatomy of a Fall*, win­ner of the Palme d’Or at Cannes. It made him re­alise, he said, that this is a golden age of cin­ema, what­ever Marvel and Bollywood sug­gest. {039-R11}

Any film, by telling a story, edits re­al­ity and sim­pli­fies the world, he said. Great art also hon­ours its com­plex­ity. *Anatomy of a Fall*, a court­room drama and a do­mes­tic drama, is lit­er­ally about that trade-off. {039-C13}
Then he turned to his co-host. If you watch one film every three years, “like Ajay Shah here”, he said, change, be­cause great art can help you un­der­stand your­self. {039-J08}
~ His part­ing ad­vice to Shah was to watch as many films as he can and skip bor­ing con­fer­ences, be­cause “all these econ­o­mists say the same damn things”.

quote.text: great art is great be­cause it ac­knowl­edges the com­plex­ity of the world.
It’s about ex­po­sure, not just of you to the world, but of the world to you. Read more, watch more, think about ideas, all of that.

p3.title: Lucky breaks
p3.deck: Four times chance found someone ready for it, and what each one teaches

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on the night Stevie Wonder lost a disc
stories.head: A missing disc and a fast car
body: *Fast Car* has been Amit Varma’s all-time favourite song since it came out in the late 1980s, though he and Tracy Chapman, he said, have noth­ing in com­mon. When she sang it at the Grammys re­cently, he re­mem­bered how the song be­came fa­mous. {039-R01}

In 1988, mas­sive crowds gath­ered for the Nelson Mandela Tribute Concert. Stevie Wonder was due on with his band. As the equip­ment was un­packed, he found that a com­puter disc with pro­grammed music he needed was not there.
Wonder said he ab­so­lutely could not per­form with­out it. According to one re­port, Varma said, he went off in tears. He was not throw­ing a tantrum, Varma added; he was re­ally upset.

The or­gan­is­ers had an empty slot and tens of thou­sands of peo­ple wait­ing. Chapman, who had played a set ear­lier to a smaller crowd, hap­pened to be around with only an acous­tic gui­tar. They asked her to fill in. {039-S03}
She sang a cou­ple of songs, one of them *Fast Car*, and it went “madly viral, as much as some­thing could go viral in the days be­fore the in­ter­net”.
Before the con­cert, her album had sold about 200,000 copies. {#sales} In the two weeks after it, it sold two mil­lion.

~ Just being there, Varma said, does not mean good things hap­pen to you. Chapman had spent thou­sands and thou­sands of hours be­com­ing good, and with­out great songs no­body would have asked her. But being there made good things more likely.
stories.why: Chance paid off only be­cause both halves were in place: the craft, and the being there. Luck, in the for­mula Varma read out, is pas­sion­ate doing mul­ti­plied by ef­fec­tive telling. {039-C01}
stories.postscript: Without that turn of events, Varma said, he might never have heard the song.

pic.caption: Amit Varma on Tracy Chapman’s lucky night

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on the hello that found the show its crew
stories.head: Hi, you’re Amit, right?
body: A few months ear­lier, Amit Varma was sit­ting in a Starbucks in Versova when a bearded man a cou­ple of ta­bles away said: “Hi, you’re Amit, right?” It was Vaibhav, who runs Chalchitra Talks. They had worked to­gether on­line but never met. {#hello}
Vaibhav, Varma said, is a nat­u­ral con­nec­tor who takes the ini­tia­tive. As they parted, Varma re­alised the show might soon need a new crew, so he took his num­ber.
When the time came, he mes­saged Vaibhav, who sent him Nomsita’s num­ber. The crew that fol­lowed, Varma said, is a bless­ing.
~ He need not have gone out that day. “I’m a clas­sic in­tro­vert,” he said. “I don’t go out much, I don’t do stuff.” {039-S05}
stories.why: A small rise in ex­po­sure can change a life in ways no­body plans. Varma was wary of mak­ing it ad­vice, though: just be­cause he got lucky, he said, does not mean you will. {#wary}

pic.caption: Amit Varma on a hello at Starbucks

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on how his father built CMIE
stories.head: The man who kept walking
body: In 1976, Ajay Shah’s fa­ther started CMIE[[x13]][[x12]], the first project of its kind he had ever done. He went out of his way to leave the house every day, meet peo­ple and cam­paign for it. {039-S04}

There was no email and there were no smart­phones. Shah’s fa­ther set up meet­ings any­way, a group of con­ver­sa­tions every day where he got to tell peo­ple what he was try­ing to do. {#smartphones}

~ His rea­son­ing was com­mon sense, Shah said. If you are build­ing an im­por­tant new or­gan­i­sa­tion, you have to go out and talk to the whole world about it, sell peo­ple on the dream and get more and more of them to join hands.
~ He had a Sanskrit proverb for it, which he often told his son.

quote.text: Charati Charato Bhaga, which trans­lates to good things hap­pen to those who walk.

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on his father’s daily rounds

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on the luckiest thing that ever happened to him
stories.head: A walk-on part in a war
body: Ajay Shah fin­ished his PhD in the United States in 1993. India’s re­forms had begun in 1991, and he had a gut in­stinct that a dra­matic time lay ahead.

He could have stayed in America. He weighed it with a lyric: “Would you ex­change a walk on part in a war for a lead role in a cage?” {039-J11} “It would be more in­ter­est­ing. It would be more chal­leng­ing. I had no idea what was going to hap­pen,” he said. He re­lo­cated to India. {039-S01}
Around that time, a team in­clud­ing R.H. Patil, Ravi Narayan and Chitra Ramakrishna was build­ing the National Stock Exchange[[x15]][[x14]]. Shah got to be a bit player in it.
~ He calls it one of the most in­ter­est­ing and ex­cit­ing times of his life. “I couldn’t ask for bet­ter,” he said.
stories.why: Shah calls it dumb luck. But the luck found him be­cause he chose the riskier, more in­ter­est­ing place to be: the episode’s theme in a sin­gle life de­ci­sion, made with­out know­ing what would come of it.

quiz.q: What did Stevie Wonder find missing before the 1988 Nelson Mandela Tribute Concert?
quiz.a: A com­puter disc with pro­grammed music he needed, so Tracy Chapman filled in.

quiz.q: In Jason Roberts’s formula as Varma read it, luck equals passionate doing multiplied by what?
quiz.a: Effective telling: the num­ber of peo­ple you ef­fec­tively com­mu­ni­cate your pas­sion to.

quiz.q: What Sanskrit proverb did Ajay Shah’s father quote while building CMIE, and what does it mean?
quiz.a: Charati Charato Bhaga: good things hap­pen to those who walk.

quiz.q: According to Ajay Shah, how is the quality of a conference panel related to fame?
quiz.a: It is in­versely pro­por­tional to the fame of the peo­ple on it.

quiz.q: Which two types from Malcolm Gladwell’s *The Tipping Point* did Amit Varma weigh himself against?
quiz.a: The maven, who goes deep, and the con­nec­tor, who links peo­ple to­gether.

quiz.q: Where was Amit Varma when a chance hello eventually found the show its new crew?
quiz.a: At a Starbucks in Versova, where Vaibhav of Chalchitra Talks said hello.

p4.credits: Everything is Everything was Amit Varma and Ajay Shah’s weekly show, 128 episodes from June 2023 to December 2025. This edition is made from Episode 39. The moving pictures, stills and chapter cards are from its video; the chapter art is by Simahina. Every play button starts the video at the moment it was said. The articles and headlines were written by Claude, an AI model, from the episode’s machine-made transcript, and checked against it. Other photographs are from Wikimedia Commons: Tracy Chapman (Hans Hillewaert, CC BY-SA 4.0); Linus Torvalds (Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0); Jimi Hendrix (A. Vente (VPRO), CC BY-SA 3.0); Richard Stallman (Patafisik, CC BY-SA 4.0); Malcolm Gladwell (PEN American Center, CC BY 2.0); Harper Lee (Eric Draper, public domain). The covers on the shelf are from Amazon, Apple and Wikipedia.

shelf.title: The Greatest Productivity Mantra: Kaator Re Bhaaji! (Episode 11)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The show’s pro­duc­tiv­ity mantra: be­tween a great idea and its re­al­i­sa­tion lies drudgery, and the rem­edy is to keep doing the work until magic hap­pens.

shelf.title: The UNIX Episode (Episode 32)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Ajay’s deep dive into the bot­tom-up story of Unix and free soft­ware, built by peo­ple work­ing for decades with no promised re­ward.

shelf.title: The Tipping Point
shelf.creator: Malcolm Gladwell
shelf.why: It helps you ask whether you are a deep spe­cial­ist or some­one who links peo­ple, and whether you should de­lib­er­ately stretch to­ward the other.

shelf.title: Even Cowgirls Get the Blues
shelf.creator: Tom Robbins
shelf.why: Ajay quotes two lines from Tom Robbins’s novel: one re­minds him that peo­ple who seem prickly are usu­ally fine once you get going, the other that stag­na­tion is a mind­set, since only those who think they are on rou­tine flights are on them.

shelf.title: To Kill a Mockingbird
shelf.creator: Harper Lee
shelf.why: Ajay read it grow­ing up as a mas­ter­piece about a par­ent and child fac­ing big­otry he as­sumed was in the past; now he finds it a hun­dred times more rel­e­vant.

shelf.title: Six Degrees
shelf.creator: Duncan Watts
shelf.why: It ex­plains how con­nected the world is, which is the sci­ence be­hind Ajay’s model of trans­mis­sion loss in human net­works.

shelf.title: Dead Poets Society
shelf.creator: Peter Weir
shelf.why: He saw it at sev­en­teen or eigh­teen, and just think­ing about it, es­pe­cially the last scene, makes him well up.

shelf.title: Anatomy of a Fall
shelf.creator: Justine Triet
shelf.why: A mas­ter­piece, Amit says, about the ten­sion be­tween telling a sim­ple, ex­plain­able story and re­spect­ing how com­plex the world is, and proof that we are in a golden age of cin­ema.

shelf.title: Anatomy of a Folly
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: It is the longer ver­sion of his ar­gu­ment about how great films bal­ance sim­pli­fy­ing a story with hon­our­ing com­plex­ity.

shelf.title: Bollywood Masala and a French Art Film
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: It is where he first ex­plored vir­tu­ous and vi­cious cy­cles, prompted by Nomsita’s re­mark that she is happy when she does things well and does things well when she is happy.

shelf.title: MAMI Film Festival
shelf.why: It is his an­nual va­ca­tion: four films a day for about ten days.

shelf.title: Amit’s MAMI live-tweet threads (2018 and 2019)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: They are a ready-made list of strong world cin­ema from those years, for view­ers who want to start watch­ing more films.

shelf.title: Magic Fruit: A Poetic Trip
shelf.creator: Vaishnav Vyas
shelf.why: A mu­si­cal play and po­etry by Vaishnav Vyas, one of the show’s young crew, which ‘ab­so­lutely blew [Amit] away’ with its cre­ativ­ity and am­bi­tion; he says it proves the young can have both youth and wis­dom.

shelf.title: Emerging Markets Conference
shelf.why: A con­fer­ence Ajay val­ues be­cause knowl­edge and ideas mat­ter there rather than a ‘great lineup of fa­mous people’; a re­cent edi­tion had a whole ses­sion on the red-hot field of the US ad­min­is­tra­tive state.

shelf.title: The Leap Blog
shelf.why: The peer-reviewed re­search blog Ajay co-edits, where his ideas are avail­able to any­one at any time.

shelf.title: XKDR Forum working papers and YouTube channel
shelf.creator: XKDR Forum
shelf.why: Ajay’s re­search or­gan­i­sa­tion, which builds a body of work in areas like law and eco­nom­ics so that the pol­icy ideas are ready when the prob­lem and the pol­i­tics line up; its work­ing pa­pers and YouTube chan­nel are where he points peo­ple who ask him to teach.

shelf.title: Ajay Shah’s writings for mass media
shelf.creator: Ajay Shah
shelf.why: This is an­other of the out­lets that give his ideas a broad au­di­ence so he can pro­tect his time for deep work.

shelf.title: The India Uncut Newsletter
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Amit’s news­let­ter, where he thinks through ideas like vir­tu­ous and vi­cious cy­cles be­fore they reach the show.

shelf.title: The Art of Clear Writing
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Amit’s writ­ing course, which treats clear writ­ing as a test of clear think­ing.

laughs.text: Amit’s open­ing thank-you: there are ‘eighty-four tril­lion videos on YouTube’ and ‘eight bil­lion peo­ple on this earth, con­stantly in­creas­ing that num­ber be­cause we are a horny species. And yet you’re watch­ing Ajay Shah and me.’

Ajay on fa­mous pan­el­lists: once they go on a con­fer­ence stage, ‘you end up hav­ing to say world peace.’ Such star-studded events, he says, ‘are for CII and FICCI to do, but not for the Indian in­tel­lec­tual com­mu­nity.’
Ajay on young­sters who want to join an open-source project for three months to put GitHub on their résumé: ‘And I just want to kick them out of the of­fice that noth­ing works like that.’
Ajay on the ‘con­tent-free hus­tlers who are just try­ing to go out and schmooze and ac­tu­ally know noth­ing.’

Ajay’s zero-transmission-loss world: Jimi Hendrix steps out of his bath­room, plays for one per­son and runs back in, ‘be­cause then you’re done, then Putin knows.’ Amit later adds that Ajay is surely two de­grees from Putin, ‘though why you should want that kind of prox­im­ity...’
After Ajay says Amit knows when he’s speak­ing with dead in­tent: ‘You are al­ways dead se­ri­ous with me, as I’m sure. And I’m never dead se­ri­ous with you. So I’m glad we got that sorted out.’

Amit roasts his co-host: watch world cin­ema even ‘if you watch one film every three years like Ajay Shah here.’ Later: ‘Increase your sur­face area of serendip­ity, Ajay Shah, by watch­ing as many films as you can, don’t go to bor­ing con­fer­ences. All these econ­o­mists say the same damn things.’

Amit calls the young crew on cam­era, ‘Run, run. Run faster... Stop run­ning,’ then cred­its them for ev­ery­thing good about the show: ‘All the credit goes here, some of it to me, none of it to Ajay.’

Amit’s pitch for Magic Fruit: watch it so that ‘thirty years later, forty years later, per­haps ninety years later, if you’re thirty and you live till one twenty, you’ll be able to tell peo­ple I was there.’
Ajay ex­plains mov­ing back to India in 1993 with the lyric: ‘Would you ex­change a walk on part in a war for a lead role in a cage?’
Richard Stallman’s line ‘a good pro­gram­mer will never starve,’ which Ajay uses to argue that a day job can co­ex­ist with a se­ri­ous craft.
Ajay ac­cepts the role of luck with a song lyric: ‘I don’t know why for­tune smiles on some and lets the rest go free.’
Amit ex­plains his in­tro­vert re­luc­tance with Sartre: ‘hell is other peo­ple.’
‘There are no strangers, there are just friends you don’t have yet,’ at­trib­uted to Tom Robbins’s Even Cowgirls Get the Blues.
